title: Mussar and Hasidism
hookLine: Mussar and Hasidism were once rivals; many now learn from both
carry: depart from evil, and do good: both halves

cards: Two people want the same thing: to become better. One keeps a small notebook.
Every night she writes down where she lost her temper, where she was stingy, where she told a little lie, and she works on one trait at a time, patiently, for weeks. The other one sings.
He dances at the Shabbat table, he looks for God in the bread and the work, and he trusts that joy will carry him upward. Both are serious. Both are Jewish paths.
For a long time, their followers eyed each other across the room.

teach.b: Two paths inward. First, the word mussar. In the book of Proverbs it means instruction, discipline: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father."
The Mussar movement took that word as its name. It grew among Lithuanian Jews around Rabbi Israel Salanter and his students, and later took root in the yeshivas.
Its tools are plain: study a little ethical teaching every day, take an honest accounting of the soul, called cheshbon hanefesh, and work on your traits, your middot, one at a time.
Second, the Hasidic path, which you've walked this whole block: joy, clinging to God, service through ordinary life, the rebbe and the song. Third, the rivalry. These grew up in different worlds.
The Lithuanian yeshivas came out of communities that had opposed Hasidism, and each side could find the other too cold or too loose, too gloomy or too carefree.

teach.h: DEPART FROM EVIL, AND DO GOOD.
teach.b: One way people describe the difference uses a single verse from the Psalms: "Depart from evil, and do good." Mussar tends to start with the first half, facing your faults squarely.
Hasidism tends to start with the second, doing good and letting the darkness fall away. Fourth, today. The old lines have softened.
Some teachers now draw on both: the notebook and the song, the honest accounting and the joy.
Heard together, they sound less like rivals and more like two halves of the same verse.
Neither one has to win for you to learn from either.

how: Students of Mussar study short ethical texts daily, keep a cheshbon hanefesh, an evening accounting of the soul, and work on one trait at a time, often with a study partner or group; Hasidim pursue inner growth through prayer, song, joy and a rebbe's teaching.

games.q: the verse says "depart from evil, and do good." which half does Mussar tend to start with?
o: depart from evil: face your faults.
do good: let joy carry you.
games.why: Mussar tends to start by facing faults squarely; Hasidism tends to start with doing good. together they make the whole verse.

practice: First try the notebook: look honestly at one trait you'd like to work on, patience, generosity, honesty, and name it without beating yourself up.
Then try the song: remember one good thing you did recently, however small, and let yourself be glad of it. Feel the difference between the two, then just breathe with both.

wordCard.voice: Two paths inward. Mussar's honest accounting and work on character, and Hasidism's joy and closeness to God: once rivals, now learned side by side by some. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: instruction, discipline, as in Proverbs' "the instruction of thy father".

carryVoice: Your line: depart from evil, and do good: both halves. Mussar's notebook and Hasidism's song can share one table. Rest well.
